answers.implementation_then_now: For both dates there is no documented pattern of state interference with migrants' religious practice. The US State Department's 2023 religious-freedom report on Chile describes constitutional and legal protection, with incidents involving non-state actors (church arsons, antisemitic statements) but no restrictions aimed at migrants. Nothing indicates a shift between 2023 and 2026, so 'Usually' is kept for both dates. The evidence is about the general population, not migrants specifically.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The citation points to Art. 19 No. 12 (expression). Freedom of conscience, belief and worship is in Art. 19 No. 6: 'La libertad de conciencia, la manifestación de todas las creencias y el ejercicio libre de todos los cultos...'. The answer 'Yes' holds, but on No. 6, read with Ley 21.325 art. 13 and art. 1(7), which names 'la religión o creencia' as a ground of arbitrary discrimination.
answers.notes: Art. 19 opens 'La Constitución asegura a todas las personas', which covers all migrants regardless of status. No court ruling was relied on.

answers.implementation_then_now: No source was found documenting interference with migrants' freedom to hold opinions, either before 2023 or in 2023-2025. The broader reports read (HRW World Report 2024, Amnesty 2025) record hostile discourse against migrants and bills to criminalise them, but no sanctions for holding opinions. The rating 'Usually' is kept for both dates on thin evidence.

answers.implementation_then_now: In both periods migrants speak and protest publicly. HRW's World Report 2024 documents a May 2023 migrant protest at the Arica border, and Amnesty (2025) documents civil-society advocacy by migrant organisations. No censorship or punishment of migrants for their expression is documented. Hostile political discourse grew in 2025, but that is not state restriction of migrants' expression. 'Usually' is kept for both dates.

answers.implementation_then_now: Because the starting protection answer is 'No', implementation is 'Does Not Apply' on both dates. No event in the window changed union or association rules for migrants: Ley 20.500 has a single version (2011), and none of the 21.325 amendments read touch arts. 13-14.
answers.sourcing_note: Ley 20.500's LeyChile page shows 'Versión: Única - 16-FEB-2011', so it is unchanged. Constitution art. 19 Nos. 15 and 19 were read on a mirror. The Código del Trabajo was not read.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'No' rests on the claim that irregular migrants cannot join trade unions. I found no provision saying so. Ley 21.325 art. 14 provides 'Los extranjeros gozarán de los mismos derechos en materia laboral que los chilenos' and obliges employers to meet labour obligations 'sin perjuicio de la condición migratoria irregular del extranjero contratado'. Art. 1(7) lists 'la sindicación o participación en organizaciones gremiales' as a ground of arbitrary discrimination. Constitution art. 19 Nos. 15 and 19 protect 'todas las personas'. A 'Yes' may be warranted. The Código del Trabajo was not read, so the original coder's reason is not disproved.
answers.notes: The starting answer is kept on both dates as instructed; the disagreement above is not a change in the law.

answers.implementation_then_now: Migrants assemble publicly in both periods. HRW's World Report 2024 records a May 2023 protest by stranded migrants at the Chile-Peru border near Arica, where police detained a man for blocking the highway. HRW also documents ongoing excessive force and weak oversight of the Carabineros in protest policing generally. Amnesty (2025) notes long states of emergency restricting assembly in the south, which mainly affects Indigenous people, not migrants specifically. No shift specific to migrants is documented, so 'Sometimes; Usually' is kept for both dates.

answers.implementation_then_now: Before 2023, CERD (Sept 2022, read through the Canadian IRB summary) found rising hate speech, xenophobic violence, excessive police force against migrants, and regular racial profiling of migrant and Afro-descendant communities by police. In 2023-2025, HRW (2024) documents obstacles to regularisation and the militarised northern border. Amnesty (2025) documents deepening hostile discourse and bills to criminalise migrants and to restrict social benefits for irregular migrants; none had become law by 1 January 2026. The pattern is the law honoured in the main with documented gaps, unchanged across the window. 'Usually' is kept for both dates, at the lower edge.

practice_sources.title: IRB Canada RIR on Chile (summarising CERD/C/CHL/CO/22-23, 2022)
Human Rights Watch World Report 2024: Chile

answers.sourcing_note: Today's text of arts. 1(7), 3 and 13 was read on LeyChile. The 2023 text is rebuilt from the amending acts (21.590, 21.589, 21.610, 21.655 read; 21.730's provisions on 21.325 not visible). The CERD findings were read second-hand through the IRB summary.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The citation relies on arts. 3 and 13 but leaves out the clearest basis: Ley 21.325 art. 1 No. 7 defines arbitrary discrimination to include distinctions 'cuando se funden en motivos como la raza o etnia, la nacionalidad, situación migratoria...'. Art. 13 lets foreigners affected by 'una discriminación arbitraria' bring 'las acciones que correspondan'. The 'Yes' holds.
answers.notes: Art. 3: 'El Estado deberá proteger y respetar los derechos humanos de las personas extranjeras que se encuentren en Chile, sin importar su condición migratoria'. The migration-law reform bill (boletín 16.072) that Amnesty criticised did not appear in the LeyChile version history before 1 January 2026.
